eras/apostolic-age/summary: The followers of Jesus of Nazareth, proclaiming him crucified, risen and Messiah, formed communities first in Jerusalem and then across the eastern Mediterranean. Under leaders such as Peter, James and Paul, the movement wrestled with whether Gentile converts must keep the Mosaic law, a question addressed at the Council of Jerusalem (c. 49). Nero's persecution in Rome (64) and the Roman destruction of Jerusalem (70) reshaped the movement, accelerating its separation from Judaism. By the end of the century the writings later gathered into the New Testament were circulating, and churches existed from Syria and Asia Minor to Rome and probably Egypt.
eras/apostolic-age/keyThemes/0: Resurrection proclamation and early worship of Jesus
eras/apostolic-age/keyThemes/1: Jewish roots and the Gentile mission
eras/apostolic-age/keyThemes/2: Paul's letters and the shape of the first churches
eras/apostolic-age/keyThemes/4: Formation of the Gospels and apostolic writings
eras/apostolic-age/globalNotes/0/text: Syriac tradition traces the faith in Edessa (Urfa) to Addai (Thaddeus), sent after the Abgar correspondence; the legend is late, but Jewish communities in Adiabene and Mesopotamia offered early bridges eastward.
eras/apostolic-age/globalNotes/1/text: The St Thomas Christians of Kerala hold that the apostle Thomas landed at Muziris c. 52 and was martyred near Mylapore c. 72; the tradition is ancient though not independently verifiable, and Roman–Indian sea trade makes a first-century contact plausible.
eras/apostolic-age/globalNotes/2/text: Acts 8 records the baptism of a court official of the Kandake (queen) of Kush (Meroë), often read as the first African convert beyond Egypt, though no lasting church in Nubia is known from this period.
eras/apostolic-age/globalNotes/3/text: Coptic tradition names Mark the Evangelist as founder of the church of Alexandria; the city's large Jewish population makes an early Christian presence likely, but firm evidence comes only in the second century.
eras/apostolic-age/globalNotes/4/text: Paul reports going to 'Arabia' (the Nabataean region) after his conversion (Galatians 1:17), and Arabs are listed among the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:11).
eras/apostolic-age/globalNotes/5/text: The Armenian Church venerates the apostles Thaddeus and Bartholomew as its first evangelists, a tradition that later gave it the name 'Apostolic'.
eras/apostolic-fathers/summary: In the generation after the apostles, writers such as Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp of Smyrna urged unity around bishops, the Eucharist and the apostolic teaching. Apologists like Justin Martyr defended the faith before pagan critics, while sporadic local persecution produced honoured martyrs. The church defined itself against rival movements—Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament, various Gnostic systems and the New Prophecy of Montanus—and in response Irenaeus articulated the 'rule of faith', apostolic succession and an emerging fourfold Gospel canon. By 200 a recognisable network of episcopally led churches stretched from Lyon to Edessa.
eras/apostolic-fathers/keyThemes/0: Bishops, presbyters and the monarchical episcopate
eras/apostolic-fathers/keyThemes/1: Apologetics and engagement with Greek philosophy
eras/apostolic-fathers/keyThemes/3: Responses to Marcion, Gnosticism and Montanism
eras/apostolic-fathers/keyThemes/4: The rule of faith and the emerging New Testament canon
eras/apostolic-fathers/globalNotes/0/tex: Tatian, a Syrian student of Justin, returned east and composed the Diatessaron (c. 170), a Gospel harmony that became the standard Gospel text of Syriac-speaking churches for centuries.
eras/apostolic-fathers/globalNotes/1/tex: The Chronicle of Edessa records a church building in Edessa destroyed by flood in 201, evidence of an established community; the Odes of Solomon, an early Syriac hymnbook, likely dates from this century.
eras/apostolic-fathers/globalNotes/2/tex: Alexandria became an intellectual centre: Pantaenus led a catechetical school there (c. 180) and Bishop Demetrius (from 189) organised the Egyptian church; papyrus fragments such as P52 show Gospels circulating in Egypt.
eras/apostolic-fathers/globalNotes/3/tex: Eusebius reports that Pantaenus travelled to 'India' (perhaps southern Arabia or India proper) and found there a Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew letters left by Bartholomew.
eras/apostolic-fathers/globalNotes/4/tex: The Scillitan Martyrs (180), executed at Carthage, left the earliest dated Christian document in Latin, signalling the rise of a Latin-speaking African church.
eras/apostolic-fathers/globalNotes/5/tex: The Quartodeciman controversy over dating Easter pitted the churches of Asia, following John's tradition, against Bishop Victor of Rome (c. 190).
eras/persecution-early-theology/summary: The third century brought the first empire-wide persecutions, under Decius (250) and Valerian (257–258), culminating in the Great Persecution launched by Diocletian in 303. Disputes over readmitting lapsed Christians led to rigorist schisms (Novatian) and debates on baptism (Cyprian), foreshadowing the Donatist crisis. Theologians such as Tertullian, Origen and Hippolytus developed the language of Trinity, Logos and scriptural interpretation, while modalist and adoptionist views (Sabellius, Paul of Samosata) were rejected. Despite persecution the church grew rapidly, and Armenia became the first kingdom to adopt Christianity officially (traditionally 301).

eras/persecution-early-theology/globalNo: Gregory the Illuminator baptised King Tiridates III, traditionally in 301 (many historians prefer c. 314), making Armenia the first state to adopt Christianity; Etchmiadzin became its spiritual centre.

Christians deported by Shapur I after his victories over Rome (250s–260s) settled in Persian cities, strengthening the church in the Sasanian empire; the Manichaean movement arose there in the same decades.

Antony of Egypt withdrew to the desert c. 270–285, inaugurating the eremitic monastic movement; Coptic translations of Scripture were under way, and the Coptic calendar dates its 'Era of the Martyrs' from Diocletian's accession in 284.
North Africa produced Tertullian and Cyprian of Carthage; Cyprian's councils (c. 251–256) on the lapsed and rebaptism shaped Latin ecclesiology.
The Aksumite kingdom traded widely with the Roman world; Christian merchants were present at Adulis, preparing the way for the conversion of King Ezana in the next era.
The house church at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates (c. 232–256), with its baptistery frescoes, is the earliest securely identified Christian building.
eras/imperial-church/name: The Imperial Church and the Great Councils
eras/imperial-church/summary: Constantine's support and the Edict of Milan (313) ended persecution and drew the church into partnership with the Roman state. The Arian controversy over the Son's relation to the Father led to the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), producing the Nicene Creed, while the Cappadocian Fathers refined Trinitarian language. Christological disputes followed: the Council of Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius, a decision the Church of the East did not accept. Monasticism spread from Egypt and Syria across the empire, Augustine reshaped Western theology on grace and the church, and Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion (380).
eras/imperial-church/keyThemes/1: Nicaea, Constantinople and the Nicene Creed
eras/imperial-church/keyThemes/5: Ephesus and the first lasting Christological division
eras/imperial-church/globalNotes/0/text: Frumentius, a Syrian Christian captive at the Aksumite court, converted King Ezana c. 330s and was consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, beginning the Ethiopian church's centuries-long link to the Coptic patriarchate; Ezana's coins replaced the crescent and disc with the cross.
eras/imperial-church/globalNotes/1/text: Under Shapur II (from c. 340) Persian Christians, suspected as Roman sympathisers, suffered a forty-year persecution with thousands of martyrs, including Bishop Simeon bar Sabba'e; the Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon (410) then organised the Church of the East under its catholicos and adopted the Nicene Creed.
eras/imperial-church/globalNotes/2/text: Nino, a woman evangelist, converted King Mirian III of Georgia (Iberia) c. 337; Mesrop Mashtots invented the Armenian alphabet (c. 405), and tradition also credits him with the Georgian script, enabling vernacular Bible translation.
eras/imperial-church/globalNotes/3/text: Pachomius founded communal (coenobitic) monasteries in Upper Egypt (c. 320s), and Athanasius' Life of Antony spread the monastic ideal; Shenoute of Atripe led the White Monastery, a centre of Coptic literature.
eras/imperial-church/globalNotes/4/text: Ephrem the Syrian (d. 373) in Nisibis and Edessa wrote hymns and commentaries that made Syriac poetry a major vehicle of theology; Aphrahat, 'the Persian Sage', wrote his Demonstrations within the Sasanian empire.
eras/imperial-church/globalNotes/5/text: Arab tribes on the Roman frontier received bishops, and the Arab queen Mavia (c. 375) demanded the monk Moses as bishop for her people as a condition of peace with Rome.
eras/imperial-church/globalNotes/6/text: Ulfilas (Wulfila) translated the Bible into Gothic (c. 350s), spreading a Homoian ('Arian') Christianity among the Goths that later shaped the barbarian kingdoms of the West.
eras/late-antiquity/name: Late Antiquity: Chalcedon, Division and the Rise of Islam
eras/late-antiquity/summary: The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as one person 'in two natures', a formula rejected by the Miaphysite churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia (later called Oriental Orthodox), producing the lasting division of Eastern Christianity. In the West the Roman Empire gave way to Germanic kingdoms, Benedictine monasticism and the papacy of Gregory the Great, while Irish and Anglo-Saxon missionaries evangelised northern Europe. The Arab conquests from 634 placed most of the Christian East under Muslim rule, and the iconoclast controversy in Byzantium was settled for icons at Nicaea II (787). Meanwhile the Church of the East carried the faith along the Silk Road as far as Tang China.
eras/late-antiquity/keyThemes/1: The papacy and the barbarian kingdoms
eras/late-antiquity/keyThemes/3: Christian life under early Islamic rule
eras/late-antiquity/keyThemes/5: Silk Road missions of the Church of the East
eras/late-antiquity/globalNotes/0/text: Alopen, a Church of the East monk, reached the Tang capital Chang'an in 635; Emperor Taizong permitted a monastery, and the Xi'an Stele (781) records 150 years of the 'Luminous Religion' (Jingjiao) in China.
eras/late-antiquity/globalNotes/1/text: The Nubian kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia were converted by rival Byzantine and Miaphysite missions in the 540s–570s; the Baqt treaty (652) with Arab Egypt protected Christian Nubia for some six centuries.
eras/late-antiquity/globalNotes/2/text: The 'Nine Saints', Miaphysite monks from the Roman East, arrived in Aksum in the late fifth century, founding monasteries such as Debre Damo and translating Scripture into Ge'ez.
eras/late-antiquity/globalNotes/3/text: After Chalcedon the Coptic church separated from the imperial (Melkite) hierarchy; the Arab conquest of Egypt (639–642) ended Byzantine pressure but began a long, gradual shift toward an Arabic-speaking Muslim majority.
eras/late-antiquity/globalNotes/4/text: Under the Abbasids the Church of the East's catholicos moved to Baghdad (c. 780); Timothy I (780–823) debated the caliph al-Mahdi and oversaw metropolitans from Syria to China, while Syriac Christians translated Greek philosophy into Arabic.
eras/late-antiquity/globalNotes/5/text: Jacob Baradaeus (d. 578) secretly ordained clergy across Syria, building the Miaphysite Syriac Orthodox hierarchy (hence 'Jacobite'); John of Damascus wrote in defence of icons from Umayyad-ruled Palestine.
eras/late-antiquity/globalNotes/6/text: A Christian community at Najran in South Arabia was massacred by the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas (c. 523), prompting Aksumite intervention; Christianity remained present in eastern Arabia and the Gulf into the eighth century.
